questions.q: What is the key difference between an implementation metric and an outcome metric?
options: An implementation metric measures whether a control was deployed; an outcome metric measures whether real risk actually changed as a result
Implementation metrics are only used by auditors, while outcome metrics are only used by engineers
Outcome metrics can only be collected once a year, while implementation metrics are continuous
There is no real difference — both terms describe the same kind of measurement
questions.explain: 'We rolled out Conditional Access to 100% of users' is an implementation metric — it proves effort. Mean-time-to-detect lateral movement or standing privileged access count prove effect.

questions.q: Why does the lesson treat mean time to detect (MTTD) lateral movement as one of the strongest outcome metrics for zero trust?
options: It is the only metric CISA's published model explicitly requires
It measures time, the thing an attacker needs most, and directly reflects whether movement across the environment now generates a detectable signal
It can be calculated without running any kind of exercise or test
It replaces the need to measure standing privileged access entirely
questions.explain: Before micro-segmentation and identity-aware logging, lateral movement often goes undetected for days; after it, the same movement now crosses a boundary that generates a signal, often cutting detection time to minutes.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend reporting phishing-resistant MFA coverage by population (admins, standard users, service identities) rather than as one blended percentage?
options: Blended percentages are not supported by most identity platforms
Service accounts are not covered by any maturity model pillar
A blended figure like '92% MFA coverage' can hide that the highest-risk population, such as admin accounts, is still on a phishable factor
Reporting by population is required by law in most jurisdictions
questions.explain: A blended 92% figure can hide the fact that every admin account is still using a phishable MFA factor, which is exactly the population where that gap matters most.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a rising count of segmentation policy violations caught right after rollout can actually be a good sign?
options: It means the segmentation rollout has failed and needs to be redone
It proves the environment had no prior segmentation at all
It means fewer real users are accessing the system than before
It shows the segmentation is actually detecting and blocking cross-segment attempts that previously went unnoticed on a flat network
questions.explain: A rising count of denied or flagged cross-segment attempts right after rollout usually means the segmentation is doing real work, catching traffic that would previously have moved unnoticed.

questions.q: In the lesson's before/after metric table example, what makes that format convincing to a skeptical audience?
options: It reports one impressive composite 'zero trust score' instead of several separate numbers
It relies entirely on acronyms to explain the change
It presents several independent, specific metrics, each with a believable mechanism for why it changed
It only reports metrics from before the rollout, not after
questions.explain: The table pairs each before/after number (standing admin accounts, MTTD, verified traffic %) with the specific mechanism that changed it — several independent, credible data points rather than one composite claim.
